- Wang et al. (EMNLP 2025): 原始 trace 对 SFT 帮助有限
- APPT (TSE 2024): 最近 competitor，BERT 非 decoder，无 trace
- **文献空白**：无现有工作做 compressed execution trace + SFT for binary verdict

- TraceCoder (ICSE 2026): 选择性 probe 优于全量 trace

1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	We evaluate our trace preprocessing pipeline across two research questions:
4	(1)~Do Tier~1 exception signals generalize across models of different capability?
5	(2)~What is the relative contribution of each trace component to verdict prediction accuracy?
6	All experiments use the TracePile benchmark \citep{chen2025tracepile} with $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% confidence intervals unless stated otherwise.
7	
8	\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
9	\label{sec:cross_model}
10	
11	To test whether exception-based trace compression is model-agnostic, we compare Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct under four input conditions: \texttt{exception\_only} (Tier~1 exception events), VOTA (exception + assertion-point + loop compression), \texttt{full\_trace} (complete execution trace), and \texttt{no\_trace} (source code only).
12	
13	\begin{table}[t]
14	\centering
15	\small
16	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
17	\toprule
18	\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Qwen-2.5-7B} & \textbf{DeepSeek-6.7B} & \textbf{Gap} \\
19	\midrule
20	exception\_only & \textbf{99.83}\% & 99.33\%$^\dag$ & 0.50pp \\
21	VOTA & 99.41\% & 84.45\% & 14.96pp \\
22	full\_trace & 81.76\% & N/A$^\ddag$ & --- \\
23	no\_trace & 75.13\% & 73.36\% & 1.77pp \\
24	\midrule
25	Majority baseline & 71.51\% & 71.51\% & --- \\
26	\bottomrule
27	\end{tabular}
28	\caption{Cross-model accuracy on TracePile ($N{=}1{,}190$). Qwen CIs: exception\_only [99.50, 100.00], VOTA [98.82, 99.83], full\_trace [79.70, 83.90], no\_trace [72.77, 77.48]; DeepSeek CIs: VOTA [82.60, 86.40], no\_trace [70.80, 75.70]. $^\dag$DeepSeek exception\_only reached 99.83\% at epoch~1 but degraded to 99.33\% at convergence (single seed, no CI). $^\ddag$DeepSeek full\_trace was invalidated due to an \texttt{evaluate.py} truncation mismatch between training and evaluation; see Limitations.}
29	\label{tab:cross_model}
30	\end{table}
31	
32	Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} reveals a striking asymmetry.
33	Under \texttt{exception\_only}, the cross-model gap is only 0.50 percentage points (pp), indicating that exception events carry a near-sufficient signal regardless of model capacity.
34	Under VOTA, the gap widens to 14.96pp: DeepSeek drops to 84.45\% while Qwen remains at 99.41\%.
35	This pattern suggests that processing mixed trace components (loop compressions, assertion points) demands model capability that the smaller DeepSeek lacks, whereas isolated exception events are interpretable by both models.
36

\section{Experiments}

We evaluate our trace preprocessing pipeline across two research questions:
(1)~Do Tier~1 exception signals generalize across models of different capability?
(2)~What is the relative contribution of each trace component to verdict prediction accuracy?
All experiments use the TracePile benchmark \citep{chen2025tracepile} with $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% confidence intervals unless stated otherwise.

\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
\label{sec:cross_model}

To test whether exception-based trace compression is model-agnostic, we compare Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct under four input conditions: \texttt{exception\_only} (Tier~1 exception events), VOTA (exception + assertion-point + loop compression), \texttt{full\_trace} (complete execution trace), and \texttt{no\_trace} (source code only).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Qwen-2.5-7B} & \textbf{DeepSeek-6.7B} & \textbf{Gap} \\
\midrule
exception\_only & \textbf{99.83}\% & 99.33\%$^\dag$ & 0.50pp \\
VOTA & 99.41\% & 84.45\% & 14.96pp \\
full\_trace & 81.76\% & N/A$^\ddag$ & --- \\
no\_trace & 75.13\% & 73.36\% & 1.77pp \\
\midrule
Majority baseline & 71.51\% & 71.51\% & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Cross-model accuracy on TracePile ($N{=}1{,}190$). Qwen CIs: exception\_only [99.50, 100.00], VOTA [98.82, 99.83], full\_trace [79.70, 83.90], no\_trace [72.77, 77.48]; DeepSeek CIs: VOTA [82.60, 86.40], no\_trace [70.80, 75.70]. $^\dag$DeepSeek exception\_only reached 99.83\% at epoch~1 but degraded to 99.33\% at convergence (single seed, no CI). $^\ddag$DeepSeek full\_trace was invalidated due to an \texttt{evaluate.py} truncation mismatch between training and evaluation; see Limitations.}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} reveals a striking asymmetry.
Under \texttt{exception\_only}, the cross-model gap is only 0.50 percentage points (pp), indicating that exception events carry a near-sufficient signal regardless of model capacity.
Under VOTA, the gap widens to 14.96pp: DeepSeek drops to 84.45\% while Qwen remains at 99.41\%.
This pattern suggests that processing mixed trace components (loop compressions, assertion points) demands model capability that the smaller DeepSeek lacks, whereas isolated exception events are interpretable by both models.

The \texttt{no\_trace} baseline confirms that source code alone provides limited signal (75.13\% for Qwen, 73.36\% for DeepSeek), only marginally above majority-class guessing (71.51\%).

Seed robustness for Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} was evaluated across three seeds (42, 123, 456): all three produced identical accuracy of 99.83\% with exactly two errors each ($\sigma{=}0$, $n{=}3$).

\end{tabular}

\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

Two findings stand out.
First, the Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \texttt{ae\_only} (99.92\%) and \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) are not distinguishable ($p{=}0.80$, McNemar's test), and both exceed VOTA (99.41\%, $p{=}0.01$ for \texttt{exception\_only} vs.\ VOTA).

\section{Related Work}

\subsection{Execution Traces for Code LLMs}

Execution traces have been increasingly explored as supplementary signals for code language models, but existing work focuses almost exclusively on generation tasks such as code repair and synthesis.
\cite{placeholder_WangEMNLP2025} provide the most comprehensive study to date, showing that execution trace SFT yields limited improvements for code generation across multiple settings---a finding we complement by demonstrating that traces become highly effective when the downstream task shifts from generation to classification.
\cite{placeholder_NiICML2024} use self-training on execution traces as chain-of-thought rationales, improving MBPP fix rates by 26.1\%, while \cite{placeholder_JungEMNLP2025} extract step-by-step traces via the Python debugger Snoop to construct CoT supervision.
Both treat traces as intermediate reasoning scaffolds for producing code, leaving the question of trace utility for binary judgments entirely unexamined.

A parallel line of work investigates what trace content to retain.
\cite{placeholder_FerrandoArXiv2025} show that compact scratchpads recording only changed values match or exceed full-state scratchpads, providing early evidence that value-level information is largely redundant.
\cite{placeholder_DemystifyingArXiv2025} corroborate this from the model capability side, finding that LLMs are substantially weaker at value tracking than at structural understanding.
TraceCoder \cite{placeholder_TraceCoderICSE2026} demonstrates that selective variable probing outperforms full traces by 34.43\% on Pass@1, and TraceRepair \cite{placeholder_TraceRepairArXiv2026} uses critical variable snapshots to repair 392 defects.
ND-Slicer \cite{placeholder_YadavallyFSE2024} proposes execution-aware pretraining to learn dynamic dependencies, and \cite{placeholder_PredSlicingFSE2024} introduces assertion-point slicing conceptually close to our snapshot design.
\cite{placeholder_HaqueACL2025} observe that trace benefits diminish as program complexity increases, while ET-CoT \cite{placeholder_ETCoTICML2025} pushes granularity to the sub-line level on CRUXEval.

These compression strategies all optimize traces for generation fluency.
Our work departs from this paradigm: for a classification objective with $O(1)$ output entropy, the optimal representation is not a compressed execution narrative but a decision-relevant event summary---a principle that yields 99.2\% verdict accuracy where full traces reach only 81.8\%.

\subsection{Fine-Tuning LLMs for Classification}

Adapting generative LLMs to classification raises distinct design questions around input representation and training objective.
\cite{placeholder_YousefiArXiv2025} compare embedding-based and instruction-based SFT for text classification, finding task-dependent trade-offs between the two paradigms.
FisherSFT \cite{placeholder_FisherSFTICML2025} leverages Fisher information to select maximally informative training subsets, improving sample efficiency for classification fine-tuning.
\cite{placeholder_BucherArXiv2024} show that fine-tuned small models consistently outperform zero-shot GPT-4 on classification benchmarks, reinforcing that SFT remains the dominant approach for binary prediction tasks.

None of these studies consider structured program execution data as input, nor do they examine how input granularity interacts with classification accuracy.
Our work bridges this gap by treating the trace format itself as a first-class design variable: when the task is binary verdict prediction, the choice of trace abstraction has a larger effect on accuracy (+24.1 points) than the choice of whether to include traces at all (+6.7 points).

\subsection{Code Correctness Prediction}

Predicting whether code is correct constitutes the task most directly related to ours, yet prior approaches rely on static representations.
APPT \cite{placeholder_APPTTSE2024} combines BERT embeddings with LSTM sequence modeling for automated patch correctness classification, reaching 79.7\% accuracy---the closest prior baseline to our verdict task setting.
\cite{placeholder_SpiessICSE2025} show that code generation models are poorly calibrated when repurposed for correctness judgments, motivating dedicated classification architectures over repurposed generators.
At industry scale, \cite{placeholder_FosterFSE2025} build a mutation equivalence detector at Meta achieving 0.95 precision, demonstrating that binary code judgments can reach high reliability through domain-specific design.

No prior code correctness predictor incorporates execution traces as input.
VOTA closes this gap by pairing trace abstraction with verdict-specific compression: reducing full execution traces to exception-type events raises accuracy from 75.1\% (no trace) past 81.8\% (full trace) to 99.2\%, with the exception-only variant reaching 99.83\%---indicating that for pass/fail judgments, knowing \emph{what went wrong} matters far more than knowing \emph{what happened}.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\subsection{Task Definition}
\label{sec:task}

We study \emph{verdict prediction}: given a code snippet $c$, a test input $i$, and an expected output $o_{\text{exp}}$, predict whether executing $c$ on $i$ produces $o_{\text{exp}}$.
Let $\mathbf{x} = (c, i, o_{\text{exp}})$ denote the static context and $t$ the full execution trace obtained by running $c(i)$.
Each experimental condition defines a trace preprocessing function $f$ such that the model receives $(\mathbf{x}, f(t))$ and generates a verdict $\hat{y} \in \{\text{pass}, \text{fail}\}$.

We formulate verdict prediction as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in an instruction-tuned chat format.
The model generates a single token---\texttt{pass} or \texttt{fail}---as its response, which constitutes a single token in both the Qwen and DeepSeek tokenizers used in our experiments.
This setup differs fundamentally from code generation: the output space is $O(1)$, so all task-relevant information must be extracted from the input representation.
The trace preprocessing function $f$ is therefore the primary design variable.

\subsection{Dataset}
\label{sec:dataset}

We use the verdict prediction dataset constructed by \cite{placeholder_WangEMNLP2025} from CRUXEval \citep{placeholder_GuICML2024}, a benchmark of 800 standalone Python functions designed for execution reasoning evaluation.
\cite{placeholder_WangEMNLP2025} paired each function with multiple test cases and collected line-by-line execution traces via a Python tracer, recording every executed line, variable assignment, function call, and exception event.
This produced 5{,}910 labeled examples, each containing the source code, test input, expected output, ground-truth verdict, and full execution trace.

We split the data into 4{,}720 training and 1{,}190 test examples.
The test set is pass-dominant: 71.51\% of samples have verdict \emph{pass}, establishing a majority-class baseline of 71.51\% accuracy.
This class imbalance motivates our use of per-class precision, recall, and F1 alongside overall accuracy.

\subsection{Trace Representations}
\label{sec:vota}

\paragraph{Full trace.}
The raw execution trace records every line execution, variable state, and function call in sequential order.
For models with limited context, traces are tokenized and truncated to fit a 2{,}048-token window.
We apply chat-template-aware truncation that reserves token budget for the verdict label at the sequence end, preventing the label from being right-truncated during tokenization---a failure mode that causes complete training collapse (Appendix~\ref{app:truncation}).

\paragraph{VOTA.}
Variable-Outcome Trace Abstraction (VOTA) extracts three diagnostic components from the full trace:

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt,parsep=0pt,topsep=4pt]
\item \textbf{Exception summary.}
Structured error events in the format \texttt{[ERROR] type: \textit{ExceptionType} message: \textit{msg}}.
Present only when execution raises an exception; absent for successful runs.

\item \textbf{Assertion point.}
A snapshot of the actual and expected output values: \texttt{[ASSERT] expected: \textit{X} actual: \textit{Y}}.
Captures the diagnostic moment where the execution outcome can be compared against the specification.

\item \textbf{Loop compression.}
A behavioral summary replacing repetitive per-iteration trace lines with iteration count and variable change trends (e.g., \texttt{3 iterations, result grows [2] $\to$ [2,4] $\to$ [2,4,6]}).
\end{enumerate}

VOTA is not a lossy compression of the full trace.
It performs \emph{targeted extraction}: each component isolates a specific diagnostic signal while discarding all intermediate execution state.
Prior trace compression work optimizes for generation fluency by retaining a narrative of execution \citep{placeholder_FerrandoArXiv2025,placeholder_TraceCoderICSE2026}; VOTA instead selects the minimal set of events sufficient for a binary judgment.
Figure~\ref{fig:vota_example} illustrates the transformation.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\fbox{\parbox{0.93\columnwidth}{%
\small
\textbf{Full trace} (excerpt, 847 tokens):\\[2pt]
\texttt{L2: x = [1, 2, 3]}\\
\texttt{L3: result = []}\\
\texttt{L4: for item in x: ~~\# iter 1}\\
\texttt{L5: ~~result.append(item * 2)}\\
\texttt{L4: for item in x: ~~\# iter 2}\\
\texttt{L5: ~~result.append(item * 2)}\\
\texttt{~~\ldots~(14 more lines)}\\[6pt]
\textbf{VOTA} (38 tokens):\\[2pt]
\texttt{[LOOP] L4--5: 3 iters, result}\\
\texttt{~~grows [2] $\to$ [2,4] $\to$ [2,4,6]}\\
\texttt{[ASSERT] expected: [2,4,6]}\\
\texttt{~~~~~~~~ actual: [2,4,6]}\\
\texttt{[No exception]}}}
\caption{Full trace to VOTA transformation. VOTA reduces token count by ${\sim}$20$\times$ while retaining only signals relevant to the pass/fail verdict.}
\label{fig:vota_example}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Experimental Conditions}
\label{sec:conditions}

\paragraph{Conditions.}
We evaluate seven trace conditions on Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct \citep{placeholder_Qwen25Coder} and four on DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{placeholder_DeepSeekCoder}.
Table~\ref{tab:conditions} lists all conditions.
The first four conditions are shared across both models; the remaining three---component-level ablations and a loss ablation---are evaluated on Qwen only.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lp{4.9cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Input to model} \\
\midrule
\texttt{no\_trace} & $\mathbf{x}$ only \\
\texttt{full\_trace} & $\mathbf{x} + t$, truncated to 2048 tokens \\
\texttt{VOTA} & $\mathbf{x} + \text{VOTA}(t)$ \\
\texttt{exception\_only} & $\mathbf{x}$ + exception component \\
\texttt{ae\_only}$^*$ & $\mathbf{x}$ + assertion-point component \\
\texttt{loop\_only}$^*$ & $\mathbf{x}$ + loop compression component \\
\texttt{label\_only\_loss}$^{*\dag}$ & $\mathbf{x} + t$; loss on verdict token only \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Experimental conditions. The first four are evaluated on both Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B; $^*$conditions are Qwen-only. $^\dag$\texttt{label\_only\_loss} uses the same input as \texttt{full\_trace} but restricts the training loss to the verdict token, isolating gradient dilution from information overload.}
\label{tab:conditions}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Training.}
All conditions use identical hyperparameters.
We fine-tune with LoRA \citep{placeholder_HuLoRA2022}: rank 16, $\alpha{=}32$, applied to all linear layers.
Training runs for 3 epochs with learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, per-device batch size 4, and gradient accumulation over 8 steps (effective batch size 32).
Maximum sequence length is 2{,}048 tokens.
Gradient checkpointing is enabled for all runs.
The primary seed is 42; we run two additional seeds (123, 456) for \texttt{exception\_only} to assess robustness of the headline result.

All experiments run on 2$\times$ NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs (96\,GB each) with CUDA 12.8.
Each single-GPU training run completes in approximately 2 hours.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report accuracy with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals ($B{=}10{,}000$).
Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap tests on per-sample predictions.
We additionally report per-class precision, recall, and F1, as well as expected calibration error \citep[ECE;][]{placeholder_NaeiniICML2015} and Brier score to assess prediction confidence.
